title: InstructGPT close read: why 1.3B parameters beat 175B — the three steps of RLHF
summary: GPT-3 could keep the thread going but not do what it was told. InstructGPT uses human-written demonstrations, human rankings, and reinforcement learning to turn it into a model that follows instructions. We unpack supervised fine-tuning, the reward model's loss function, the KL penalty, and the alignment tax, work through a few small examples by hand, and examine how the paper honestly answers: aligned to whom, exactly?
ai_summary: InstructGPT (OpenAI, 2022) turns GPT-3 into a model that follows instructions in three steps: supervised fine-tuning on about 13,000 human-written demonstrations; training a 6B reward model on labelers' rankings of 4–9 answers; then using PPO reinforcement learning to pursue high scores, with a KL penalty to prevent gaming and pretraining data mixed in (PPO-ptx) to reduce the 'alignment tax.' Labelers preferred the 1.3B-parameter InstructGPT over the 175B-parameter GPT-3; the 175B version beats GPT-3 85 ± 3% of the time, and the hallucination rate drops from 41% to 21%. Bias did not improve, and the model can be more toxic when asked to be. The paper stresses that it aligns with the preferences of specific labelers, researchers, and customers, not with 'human values.'
brief: Problem: a GPT-3 trained to predict the next token does not necessarily follow the user's intent; it hallucinates and drifts off topic.

Method: human-written demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning → human rankings of answers to train a reward model → PPO to chase high scores, with a KL penalty to rein the model in and pretraining data mixed in to reduce capability regressions.
Result: the 1.3B-parameter InstructGPT was preferred over 175B GPT-3; it hallucinates less, is less toxic when asked to be respectful, and costs only a sliver of the pretraining compute.
Limits: bias did not improve; the model follows harmful instructions and goes along with false premises; it is aligned with a small, specific group of people, not 'humanity.'

paper.title: Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback
paper.authors: Long Ouyang, Jeff Wu, Xu Jiang, Diogo Almeida, Carroll L. Wainwright, Pamela Mishkin, et al. (20 authors)

cover.headline: A close read of the InstructGPT paper

sections.h: The upshot: what this paper actually did

blocks.p: In March 2022, 20 authors from OpenAI's alignment team released this 68-page paper. The problem it solves can be stated in one line: GPT-3 is very good at **continuing text** but not very good at **doing what you ask**. Tell it to 'write a story about a frog' and it may list several similar writing prompts; ask it a question and it may fabricate an answer that looks plausible.

The paper's answer is to have people teach it: first, labelers demonstrate what a good answer should look like; then they rank several model outputs, and those rankings train a scoring **reward model**; finally, a language model uses reinforcement learning to chase high scores. This pipeline is called **reinforcement learning from human feedback** (RLHF), and the resulting model is InstructGPT.

The result was surprising: on real user prompts, labelers preferred answers from a 1.3B-parameter InstructGPT over a 175B-parameter GPT-3, even though the latter is more than 100 times larger. Head-to-head, the 175B InstructGPT beat GPT-3 85 ± 3% of the time. Its hallucination rate dropped from 41% to 21%, and the compute it cost was less than one sixtieth of training GPT-3.

ChatGPT, released eight months later, used the same recipe. Today nearly every chat model goes through some form of 'alignment' training, and this paper is the first complete account of that path working at real product scale.

callout.title: The one-sentence version
callout.text: InstructGPT = GPT-3 + three training steps: (1) supervised fine-tuning on human-written demonstrations (SFT); (2) have people rank several model answers and train a reward model (RM) to score outputs; (3) use the PPO reinforcement-learning algorithm to chase high scores, while a 'leash' (the KL penalty) keeps it from drifting off course to game the score. The paper also shows that **making the model follow instructions better is worth more than making it 100 times larger**.

callout.title: Four small concepts you need for this paper
callout.text: Don't worry if you don't know them; these four are enough:
list: **GPT-3**: a 175B-parameter language model trained to predict the next token. For what it can do and how to use it, see our GPT-3 close read.
**Fine-tuning**: taking a trained model and training it further on new data, nudging its parameters toward a new objective.

**Reinforcement learning**: the model takes an action (here, writing a response), receives a score (the reward), then adjusts itself so actions that earn higher rewards happen more often. The model being trained is called the **policy**.

**Sigmoid function σ(z)**: squashes any number into the range 0 to 1: σ(0) = 0.5, and the larger z is, the closer to 1; the smaller z is, the closer to 0. It is often used to turn a score difference into a probability.

sections.h: Problem: continuing the thread is not the same as following instructions

blocks.p: GPT-3's training objective is: given a passage from the internet, guess the next word. That objective is not the same as what we actually want — 'respond to the user's intent helpfully and safely.' The paper calls this mismatch a **misalignment** between the model and its users, and it shows up as fabricated facts, biased or toxic output, or simply not following instructions.

callout.title: Like an intern who has only memorized the internet
callout.text: You tell him, 'Help me write an apology letter.' In his head he isn't thinking 'what does the boss want?' but 'what usually follows this sentence online?' On the internet, that sentence is usually followed by another request, a forum title, or a whole list of writing prompts. He isn't trying to be difficult — nobody ever taught him that this is an instruction and he should carry it out.

blocks.p: Section 4.3 (Figure 8) gives a real example: the model was asked in French to 'write a short story about a frog that travels to ancient Greece.' GPT-3 175B did not write the story; it kept listing several similar French writing prompts. InstructGPT simply began telling the frog story in French.

So what does 'alignment' actually mean? The paper follows Askell et al.: an aligned model should be **helpful** (it should follow instructions and infer intent from a few examples or a 'Q: ... A: ...' format), **honest**, and **harmless**. But honesty is hard to test directly, because we cannot know what the model 'believes', so the paper settles for measuring **truthfulness**: whether what the model says matches the facts. Harmlessness is also hard to test, because whether a text is harmful depends on how it is used: producing profanity in a chatbot is bad, but it can be useful when training a profanity detector.

quiz.q: According to the paper, what is the root cause of GPT-3 not following instructions?
options: Too few parameters
The training objective is to predict the next token in internet text, not to act on the user's intent
The training data contains no instructions
It does not use the Transformer architecture
quiz.why: The paper's diagnosis is objective mismatch: the language-modeling objective is only a proxy for what we actually want. Parameter count is not the reason — later we will see that a 1.3B InstructGPT with the same architecture is preferred over the 175B model. The internet certainly includes instructions; the problem is that the model learns what usually follows an instruction, rather than to carry it out.

sections.h: The overall method: demonstrate, score, practice — three steps

blocks.p: The method follows OpenAI's earlier work on text continuation and summarization (Ziegler et al. 2019; Stiennon et al. 2020), and this is the first time it is applied to a broad mix of instructions. The starting point has three ingredients: a pretrained GPT-3, a pool of prompts the model should answer well, and a team of trained labelers.

fig.title: InstructGPT's three steps: first imitate, then learn to score, then train against the score
fig.subtitle: Schematic: adapted from Figure 2 and Section 3.1 of the paper; data sizes come from Section 3.2

steps.name: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)
steps.desc: Labelers hand-write an ideal answer for each prompt, and GPT-3 learns from those demonstrations.

steps.name: Training the reward model (RM)
steps.desc: The model writes 4–9 answers to the same prompt, labelers rank them from best to worst, and the reward model learns to score answers.

steps.name: Reinforcement learning (PPO)
steps.desc: The model writes answers, the reward model scores them, and the model updates toward higher scores while being kept close to the Step 1 model.

callout.title: A cooking analogy
list: **Step 1 is like apprenticing under a chef**: the chef personally cooks hundreds of dishes for the apprentice to observe, and the apprentice imitates them. This produces faithful imitation, but the chef's time is limited, so the total supply of demonstrations is never large.

**Step 2 is like training a taster**: the apprentice makes several versions of a dish, and the diners only have to rank which is better and which is worse. Ranking is much cheaper than cooking. A large set of ranking records trains a taster to predict the diners' taste.

**Step 3 is like the apprentice practicing against the taster over and over**: the taster never gets tired and can score dishes at any time; the apprentice keeps adjusting his cooking to please him. But the taster has blind spots, so the apprentice is required not to stray too far from the chef's own cooking — that is the KL penalty described later.

blocks.p: Why not stop after Step 1? Because **judging is cheaper than creating**. Writing a good answer takes minutes or more, while comparing two answers takes seconds. And many things are easier for people to judge than to write well themselves. Steps 2 and 3 turn that human ability to judge into a steady stream of training signal.

Steps 2 and 3 can also loop: use the current best model to generate new answers, collect new rankings, train a new reward model, then train a new policy. The paper says the comparison data it actually collected came mostly from SFT model outputs and partly from PPO model outputs.

The prompts came mostly from the OpenAI API Playground: text users submitted while trying early versions of InstructGPT (users were repeatedly notified that their data could be used for training). API requests made in the production product were **not** used. The processing was deliberate:

list: **Deduplication**: prompts with a long identical opening were treated as duplicates.
**At most 200 prompts per user**: this prevents a few heavy users from dominating the data.

**Split by user**: the training, validation, and test sets are divided by user ID, so users in the test set have no examples in the training set. The test results therefore measure performance on new users.
**Filter personal information**: prompts in the training set were filtered to remove personally identifiable information (PII).

blocks.p: But at the start of the project, instruction-like prompts were not yet available: users rarely wrote direct instructions to ordinary GPT-3. So the team first asked labelers to write three kinds of prompts: diverse tasks they came up with themselves, tasks with a few Q&A examples, and tasks based on the uses people described in API waitlist applications. These were used to train the first InstructGPT models, which were placed in Playground, which then produced real user instructions.

fig.title: Three datasets: SFT is mostly labeler-written; PPO is all real users
fig.subtitle: Unit: prompts in the training set. From Table 6 of the paper; amber is PPO data, which requires no human labeling at all
rows: Hand-write an answer for each prompt
fig.note: SFT has more labeler-written prompts because the early interface asked labelers to write a general instruction plus a few examples; the paper then sampled different combinations of examples from the same instruction to create multiple training examples.

blocks.p: Compared with the hundreds of billions of tokens used to pretrain GPT-3, this data is tiny: the demonstrations number just over 10,000. Later we will see that this small amount of high-quality human data changed the model's behavior. More than 96% of the data is English.
What do users actually use it for? Labelers classified the prompts in the RM dataset, and the distribution is quite different from the benchmarks common in academia:

fig.title: What real users do with GPT-3: nearly half is generation; classification and QA are only a minority
fig.subtitle: Unit: %, use-case distribution of API prompts, as judged by labelers. From Table 1 of the paper; amber is generation
fig.note: Closed QA means the answer should come only from the given material; open QA may use any knowledge.

blocks.p: **Labelers** were about 40 contractors hired from Upwork and ScaleAI. Because prompts can involve sensitive topics, the hiring process included a screening test: could they recognize potentially harmful outputs, were they sensitive to different groups of people, and did their labels agree with the researchers' labels? During the project, researchers were available in a shared chat room to answer questions.

People disagree with one another, so the team first measured how reliable the 'gold standard' labels were. Training labelers agreed with each other 72.6 ± 1.5% of the time; a separate held-out group that produced no training data and took no screening test agreed 77.3 ± 1.3%. For reference, researchers in an earlier summarization task agreed with each other 73 ± 4% of the time. In other words, roughly a quarter of comparisons are contested even among humans, so a reward model predicting human preferences can hardly be much more accurate than that.

callout.title: Priorities differ between training and evaluation
callout.text: Helping the user and avoiding harm can conflict, for example when a user requests a potentially harmful answer. The paper's approach: during **training**, labelers were told to prioritize helpfulness to the user; during **final evaluation**, labelers were told to prioritize truthfulness and harmlessness. The paper acknowledges that handling this conflict during training requires difficult design decisions and leaves it for future work.

sections.h: Step 1: supervised fine-tuning — first learn that this is an instruction

blocks.p: Step 1 is the most direct: take labeler-written demonstrations and fine-tune GPT-3 with ordinary supervised learning. The objective is still 'predict the next token', but now it is predicting the next token of a **demonstration answer**. The model thereby learns one crucial format: the prompt is a task, and what follows should be an answer that completes it.

The paper trains for 16 epochs (one full pass through all demonstrations per epoch), with cosine learning-rate decay and residual dropout of 0.2. There is a counterintuitive detail: **after only 1 epoch, validation loss starts to get worse** (overfitting); yet as training continues, both the reward-model score and human preference scores keep improving.

callout.title: Worse validation loss does not mean the model got worse
callout.text: The paper does not explain why, but one common reading is: validation loss measures how much probability the model puts on the labelers' particular demonstration. But there is more than one good answer. As the model becomes increasingly confident about one good answer, it assigns lower probability to other good answers, so loss rises even though human readers become more satisfied. That is why the paper does **not** select the model by validation loss, but by the reward model's score on the validation set. It is a reminder that the numerical metric we train on can diverge from what we actually want.

blocks.p: There is also an easy-to-miss detail (Appendix C.3): the SFT model that serves as the starting point for Step 3 is **not** the same model as the 16-epoch SFT baseline above. The reinforcement-learning starting point was trained for only 2 epochs and mixed in 10% pretraining data; the paper found this was more favorable to the PPO training that followed.

sections.h: Step 2: the reward model — turn which answer people prefer into a score

blocks.p: Reinforcement learning needs a referee that can score at any moment, but you cannot bring in a human to judge every generated answer. Step 2 therefore trains a model to **score in place of humans**: give it a prompt and an answer, and it outputs a single number; a higher score means a human is more likely to prefer that answer.

Its architecture is simple: take the SFT model, remove the final output layer that turns vectors into next-token probabilities, and replace it with a projection layer that outputs a single number. The paper uses only a 6B reward model: the 175B version was unstable to train, and because the reward model later initializes PPO's value function, a much larger model would make the compute balloon.

**Where the data comes from**: for a given prompt, generate K answers (K is between 4 and 9), and labelers rank them from best to worst. Any two of the K answers can form a 'which is better' pair, giving C(K,2) = K(K−1)/2 pairs total. A single ranking of 9 answers yields 36 comparison pairs — much cheaper than asking pairwise questions one at a time.

**How scores are learned from comparisons**: the core assumption is simple: the larger the score gap between two answers, the more likely a human is to choose the higher-scored one. That probability is modeled by passing the score difference through a sigmoid function, squashing it between 0 and 1. The training objective is to make the score of the answer the human chose as much higher as possible than the rejected answer:

parts.desc: The score the reward model assigns to answer y for prompt x; θ is the reward model's parameters
Within the same pair, the answer the labeler preferred (w for win) and the answer they liked less (l for lose)
The probability, according to the model's scores, that a person would choose y_{w}. When the score gap is 0 the probability is 0.5; the larger the gap, the closer it is to 1.
The loss for this pair: the more confident the model is that y_{w} is better, the closer the loss comes to 0; if it ranks the two the wrong way round, the loss becomes very large.
One ranking yields C(K,2) comparison pairs; dividing by it averages them, so prompts ranked with 4 answers and prompts ranked with 9 answers count equally.
Average over all comparisons in the comparison dataset D.

formula.note: The assumption of using the sigmoid of a score difference to represent preference probability is called the Bradley-Terry model in statistics, and it follows the same idea as chess Elo ratings: the larger the rating gap between two players, the higher the probability that the higher-rated one wins.

plain.title: Ranking is easier than scoring.
plain.text: Asking a labeler whether an answer deserves a 7.3 or a 7.8 is hard to do consistently; asking them to put several answers in order is much easier. One ranking (A best, D worst) decomposes into every pairwise comparison: 4 answers yield 6 pairs. The reward model learns to score from these “who beat whom” comparisons.

fig.title: Three comparisons by hand: correct rankings cost little loss, reversed rankings cost a lot.
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: scores are constructed for this example, not taken from the paper. r_{w} is the score of the answer people preferred, r_{l} the score of the rejected answer; amber marks the case where the model ranked them the wrong way.
columns: σ(gap): the probability the model assigns to a person choosing y_{w}.
rows: The model ranked them correctly and is very confident.
The model sees the two as about equal.
The model ranked them the wrong way.
fig.note: During training, comparisons like the third row produce the largest gradient, pushing the reward model to raise y_{w}'s score and lower y_{l}'s score until the ranking is correct.

blocks.p: This loss cares only about **score differences**, not the scores themselves. Add 10 points to every answer, and every pair's gap is unchanged, so the loss is exactly unchanged. The “zero point” of the scores is therefore arbitrary. Before reinforcement learning begins, the paper adds a bias that sets the zero point at the average score of the labeler demonstrations: a positive score means better than the average demonstration, a negative score worse.

**An engineering detail that made training work**: the 36 comparison pairs from one ranking are highly correlated, since they all compare the same set of answers. The paper initially shuffled all comparisons together, and the reward model overfit after just one pass through the data: each answer appears in K−1 pairs, so it was effectively learned K−1 times. Once all comparisons for the same prompt were grouped together as a single training sample, the overfitting disappeared and validation accuracy improved substantially; each answer also only had to be read once by the reward model, saving compute. Under this scheme, a batch of 64 prompts contains up to 64 × 36 = 2,304 comparison pairs.
The reward model is trained for only 1 epoch: more epochs quickly overfit. Its learning rate, by contrast, is not very sensitive—changing it by 50% leaves results about the same.

**Can the reward model represent other people's tastes?** The paper splits labelers into 5 groups, trains on data from 4 groups each time, and tests on the held-out group. When predicting the preferences of the **unseen group**, accuracy is 69.6 ± 0.9%; for the people in the training groups it is 72.4 ± 0.4%. That is only slightly lower, and already close to the roughly 73% agreement rate between humans.

quiz.q: A labeler ranks K = 4 answers. How many comparison pairs does that produce?
options: 3 pairs
4 pairs
6 pairs
12 pairs
quiz.why: The pairs are formed by choosing any two answers: C(4,2) = 4 × 3 ÷ 2 = 6. Three pairs would only compare adjacent ranks, wasting the information in the ranking; twelve pairs would count both “A beats B” and “B beats A” separately.

quiz.q: If you add 10 to the reward model's score for every answer, what happens to the training loss?
options: It increases.
It decreases.
It stays exactly the same.
It cannot be computed.
quiz.why: Only the score difference r_{w} − r_{l} appears in the loss; adding 10 to all scores leaves the difference unchanged, so both σ and the loss stay the same. This is why the paper adds an extra bias to set the average demonstration score to 0: the loss itself does not determine the zero point.

sections.h: Step 3: Reinforcement learning, with a leash

blocks.p: With a reward model that can score, Step 3 has the language model chase high scores. The paper designs this as the simplest possible reinforcement-learning environment (called a bandit environment): pick a random user prompt, have the model write a response, get one score from the reward model, and the episode ends. There is no multi-turn dialogue and no intermediate reward.

The algorithm used to update the model is PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization, Schulman et al. 2017). Its key idea: each update is not allowed to change the model too much; any step beyond a set fraction is clipped (the paper's clipping fraction is 0.2), which makes training more stable.

But there is a big trap here. The reward model is only a **proxy** for human preferences; it has seen only tens of thousands of prompts and has its own blind spots. If the language model is optimized hard enough, it will find those blind spots, producing things the reward model scores highly but a person finds baffling. This is called **over-optimizing** the reward model, like a student studying the grader's habits to inflate scores rather than actually solving the problems.

callout.title: The kite string
callout.text: The solution is to tie the model to a leash: for each word it writes, compare the probability the RL model assigns to that word with the probability the original SFT model assigns. The further it drifts, the more gets docked. The model can fly toward higher scores, but not far—it stays near the territory of human-written demonstrations. This penalty term measures the difference between two probability distributions and is called the **KL divergence** penalty.

blocks.p: With the leash, plus the “pretraining review” described later, the objective maximized in Step 3 is:

formula.expr:
objective(φ) = E_{(x,y)∼RL} [ r_{θ}(x, y)
    − β · log( π^{RL}_{φ}(y | x) / π^{SFT}(y | x) ) ]
    + γ · E_{x∼pretrain} [ log π^{RL}_{φ}(x) ]

parts.desc: The language model being trained (the policy), with parameters φ.
The SFT model from Step 1, held fixed and serving as the other end of the leash.
An expectation over randomly drawing a user prompt x and having the model being trained write an answer y.
The reward model's score for that answer.
How much more probable this answer is under the new model than under the SFT model, in log terms; summed over words, this is the KL penalty for the answer.
The tightness of the leash; the paper uses 0.02.
The second line: sample text x from GPT-3's pretraining data and continue doing next-token prediction; γ controls its weight. When γ = 0 the method is called PPO; when γ > 0 it is called PPO-ptx.

formula.note: The paper says that, unless stated otherwise, InstructGPT refers to the PPO-ptx model throughout.

plain.title: The score, minus the penalty for drifting off course, plus keeping old skills intact.
plain.text: During reinforcement learning, the model maximizes the sum of three things: the reward model's score (as high as possible), minus the penalty for straying too far from the original model (β · KL), plus a bit of the original pretraining practice (the γ term). That last term exists to pay less of the “alignment tax” and avoid forgetting old skills.

fig.title: KL penalty by hand: a reward 1 point higher can still lose out if the drift is too far.
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: numbers are constructed for this example, not taken from the paper. β = 0.02; the “sum of log probability ratios” is computed for each word in the answer as the ratio of the new model's probability to the SFT model's probability, logged and summed. Amber marks the answer with the higher final score.
rows: B: a weird answer that exploits the reward model's blind spots
fig.note: The per-word penalty is small: if the SFT model gives a word probability 0.1 and the RL model gives it 0.4, log(0.4/0.1) ≈ 1.39; multiplied by 0.02, that docks only 0.028 points. But if many words in an answer diverge substantially, the penalty accumulates and can override a high reward-model score.

blocks.p: Other key settings: PPO trains for a total of 256k episodes, using about 31k deduplicated, PII-removed prompts; each batch has 512 episodes, split into 8 minibatches, each trained on once. Policies of all sizes use the same 6B reward model, and it is also used to initialize the 6B value function (an auxiliary model PPO needs to estimate roughly what score an answer will get). That way models of different sizes share the same referee, making comparisons fairer.

quiz.q: If the KL penalty coefficient β is set to 0, what is most likely to happen?
options: The model stops learning.
The model will exploit the reward model's blind spots: reward scores keep rising, but human evaluations may not improve.
The model will regress back to GPT-3.
Nothing changes.
quiz.why: β = 0 means cutting the leash: the model only tries to please the reward model. The reward model is an imperfect proxy, and under heavy optimization its blind spots are exposed—that is over-optimization. The model does not stop learning, and it does not regress to GPT-3, because nothing pulls it back.

sections.h: The alignment tax: more obedient, but some old abilities slip.

blocks.p: Training with PPO alone revealed a problem: the model got worse on some public NLP benchmarks, including reading comprehension SQuAD and DROP, commonsense reasoning HellaSwag, and WMT 2015 French-to-English translation. The paper calls this cost the **alignment tax**: some capability is sacrificed in exchange for alignment.

Why does this matter? If alignment carries a heavy tax, people will prefer a less aligned but more capable model, and alignment methods will not spread. So the paper treats reducing the alignment tax as part of the method itself.

The solution is the PPO-ptx term in the second line of the objective: after each PPO update, the model also takes one next-token-prediction update on GPT-3's original pretraining data—like learning new rules while reviewing old material. The number of pretraining samples is 8 times the number of RL episodes, with the gradient multiplied by γ = 27.8.

fig.title: Alignment tax: with PPO alone reading comprehension drops sharply; mixing in pretraining recovers most of it.
fig.subtitle: 175B model, zero-shot. From Table 14 in the paper appendix; HellaSwag is accuracy (%), the others are F1 or BLEU. Blue columns are InstructGPT (PPO-ptx).
fig.note: PPO-ptx even surpasses GPT-3 on HellaSwag, but still trails on DROP, SQuADv2, and translation. The paper says “most” of the regressions were mitigated, not all of them eliminated.

plain.title: Practicing the specialty without losing the basics.
plain.text: With reinforcement learning alone, the model became better at following instructions but lost old abilities like reading comprehension—like drilling exam technique until the fundamentals get rusty. The paper's remedy is to mix some original pretraining data into training, which is like continuing to read normally while practicing the specialty; most of the regression is recovered.

blocks.p: One small issue we noticed while reading the table: in the same appendix Table 14, the ROUGE-L scores for the CNN/DM and TL;DR summarization tasks are identical for all 12 numbers. Two different datasets are unlikely to produce exactly identical results; the rows were probably copied incorrectly during typesetting, so be careful when citing them.

**Why not simply tighten the leash (increase β)?** Intuitively, the closer the model stays to SFT, the fewer abilities it should lose. The paper tried this on the 1.3B model: raising β to 2.0, 100 times the default, still did not fully restore DROP and SQuAD, while reward scores clearly dropped. With pretraining data mixed in, however, there is a γ value that both reverses the regression and barely lowers reward scores. The paper also tried moving the other end of the leash from the SFT model to GPT-3 itself, with similar results, and concluded that the distribution of pretraining data is what matters. Our reading: the KL penalty constrains the model's outputs only on user prompts, while abilities like reading comprehension show up on completely different inputs, where the leash cannot reach. Reviewing pretraining data directly is what covers them.

Another warning: on the 1.3B model, extending training from 256k to 512k episodes caused DROP and SQuADv2 to start out better than GPT-3, then decline the longer training ran, ending slightly below GPT-3. The alignment tax accumulates with training time.

quiz.q: To reduce the alignment tax, why does the paper choose to mix in pretraining data (PPO-ptx) rather than increase the KL coefficient β?
options: Because increasing β slows training.

Because even raising β to 100 times its default fails to recover the regression, while clearly lowering reward scores; mixing in pretraining data recovers the regression while barely lowering reward scores.
Because pretraining data is cheaper.
Because β cannot be greater than 1.
quiz.why: This is the ablation conclusion from Appendix E.6. Increasing β only pulls the model toward the SFT model, and the SFT model itself already trails GPT-3, so that cannot recover the gap; it also sacrifices alignment quality. Speed, cost, and β's allowed range are not reasons given by the paper.

sections.h: Result one: people prefer it, and the small model beats the big one.

blocks.p: The main evaluation asks labelers to look at different models' answers to the same prompt and judge which they prefer, while also scoring each answer from 1 to 7 and flagging specific problems (such as failing to follow the instruction or fabricating content). The test prompts come from **users who do not appear in the training data**.

Besides GPT-3, SFT, and PPO, the comparison includes one carefully built baseline: GPT-3 with a deliberately designed few-shot prefix to put it into “follow instructions” mode (GPT-3-prompted). The prefix was chosen through a contest between two authors: each spent an hour interacting with GPT-3, produced their two best prefixes, and the winner was decided by the reward model's validation-set scores. The footnote says only: author DA won.

The result is a clear ladder: GPT-3 is worst; adding a good few-shot prefix is clearly better; supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations is another step better; and PPO on comparison data is better still. Whether or not pretraining data is mixed into PPO makes little difference to human preferences.

fig.title: How often the 175B InstructGPT was chosen against each opponent in head-to-head comparisons.
fig.subtitle: Unit: %, labeler preferences on API prompts; after ± is the margin of error. From Sections 1 and 4.1 of the paper; amber is against the original GPT-3.
fig.note: 50% means a tie. FLAN and T0 are 175B GPT-3 models that were instruction-tuned on many public NLP tasks; they are covered separately below.

blocks.p: The most striking comparison is size: **the 1.3B-parameter InstructGPT is preferred over the 175B-parameter GPT-3**, even though the two have exactly the same architecture and differ only in that InstructGPT was fine-tuned on human data. Adding a few-shot prefix to GPT-3 does not change the conclusion.

Beyond “which one do you prefer?”, labelers also flagged more specific problems. Compared with GPT-3, InstructGPT was more appropriate as a customer-service assistant, more often obeyed explicit constraints in instructions (such as “answer in no more than two paragraphs”), less often failed the task entirely, and fabricated less often on closed-domain tasks:

fig.title: Fabrication rate on closed-domain tasks: down from 41% to 21%.
fig.subtitle: Unit: %. Closed-domain tasks are tasks where the answer should come only from the given material, such as summarization or answering questions from a passage. From Section 1 of the paper; amber is InstructGPT.

blocks.p: **Did it merely learn to please those 40 people?** The paper checks this two ways: first, it asks held-out labelers who did not contribute training data to evaluate, and they also strongly prefer InstructGPT; second, there is the reward-model cross-validation described earlier. Both suggest the model did not just learn to please the few people who trained it. But those “other” people come from the same contracting channels as the training labelers, and the paper says how broader populations would react still needs research.

The paper also evaluated on a different set of prompts: prompts users submitted to ordinary GPT-3 (rather than instruction-style prompts written for InstructGPT). The conclusions were largely unchanged, though PPO-ptx was slightly worse at the largest size.

callout.title: Alignment is much cheaper than scaling.
callout.text: Training the 175B SFT model took 4.9 petaflop/s-day; training the 175B PPO-ptx took 60 petaflop/s-day; and training GPT-3 itself took 3,640 petaflop/s-day. In other words, for less than one-sixtieth of GPT-3's compute, the gain is larger than making the model 100 times bigger. The paper concludes that, at least for the tasks customers actually use, investing in aligning existing models is a better deal than training larger ones.

fig.title: Alignment compute is only a fraction of pretraining.
fig.subtitle: Unit: petaflop/s-day (one quadrillion floating-point operations per second for one day). From Section 5.1 of the paper; amber is GPT-3 pretraining.
fig.note: This counts model training only; the human cost of collecting data is separate. The paper says that, including experiments, the total cost is still only a small fraction of training GPT-3.

sections.h: Why FLAN and T0 trained on public tasks aren't enough.

blocks.p: Around the same time, academia was pursuing “instruction tuning”: rewriting many public NLP datasets into instruction–answer form and training on them, with FLAN and T0 as prominent examples. The paper took about 1 million examples from each of these two datasets, fine-tuned 175B GPT-3 on them separately, and compared the results.

The result: they beat the original GPT-3 and perform about as well as GPT-3 with a well-crafted few-shot prefix, but worse than the SFT baseline. Measured as win rate against the 175B SFT baseline, InstructGPT scores 73.4 ± 2%, the T0 version 26.8 ± 2%, and the FLAN version 29.8 ± 2%.

The paper gives two reasons. First, public datasets are designed for **easy automatic scoring**, so they skew toward tasks with standard answers, like classification and QA. But for real users, classification and QA together account for only about 18%, while open-ended generation and brainstorming account for about 57% (see the use-case distribution above). Second, public datasets rarely match the richness of real user inputs.

callout.title: That does not mean FLAN and T0 are useless.
callout.text: The paper's conclusion is measured: public NLP tasks are also instructions, and models should be expected to handle them. **The broadest instruction-following models should combine both kinds of data.** What is compared here is "which model is preferred on real user prompts," which is different from academic benchmarks.

sections.h: Result two: more truthful, toxicity dips slightly, bias does not improve.

blocks.p: **Truthfulness.** TruthfulQA is a set of questions designed specifically to lure models into saying the wrong thing (for example by exploiting common misconceptions), and the paper had humans judge whether answers were truthful and informative. The conclusion: PPO models produce answers that are both truthful and informative about twice as often as GPT-3, and this is default behavior—no need to coax the model to "tell the truth." The exception is the 1.3B PPO-ptx, which does slightly worse than a same-size GPT-3.

If the prompt adds a line like "answer 'I have no comment' if you are unsure," PPO models are more inclined to say "I have no comment" than to state something wrong with confidence; GPT-3 does worse here.

fig.title: TruthfulQA automatic scores: PPO models improve a lot, but these numbers are inflated.
fig.subtitle: 175B models, ordinary QA prompts. From Appendix Table 14 (automatic scores, not human judgments); amber is InstructGPT (PPO-ptx).
fig.note: The paper's acknowledgments note that the TruthfulQA dataset authors said the automatic scores overstate PPO models' improvement. That is why the main text uses human judgment and reports about "twice," not the nearly threefold gap in this table.

callout.title: Two places where the paper is not fully consistent.
list: The introduction says results are "equally strong" on the subset of questions not adversarially selected against GPT-3; Section 4.2 says PPO models are still significantly better on that subset, but the absolute improvement is a few percentage points smaller.

The introduction says "about twice," based on human judgment; Appendix Table 14's automatic scores show nearly threefold, and the paper itself admits the automatic scores overstate the improvement. When reading the numbers, be clear which scoring method is being used.

blocks.p: **Toxicity.** The team tested with the RealToxicityPrompts dataset (a set of sentence beginnings likely to elicit profanity), using both the automated Perspective API scorer and human judgment. To get more high-toxicity inputs, the paper sampled prompts uniformly by toxicity, so absolute toxicity numbers run higher than under the usual sampling. The results fall into three cases:

fig.title: When asked to be respectful, toxicity drops; when asked to be toxic, it is more toxic than GPT-3.
fig.subtitle: Average Perspective API toxicity score for 175B models (0 to 1, higher is more toxic). From Appendix Table 14; amber is prompts requesting bias.
rows: Asked to be polite and respectful
fig.note: The introduction says that when asked to be respectful, InstructGPT produces about 25% fewer toxic outputs than GPT-3; this table uses a different average-score metric, falling from 0.233 to 0.196. With no instruction, the two are about the same.

blocks.p: Human evaluation agrees: InstructGPT is less toxic when asked to be respectful, and about the same as GPT-3 when no instruction is given. The SFT model is the least toxic, but its answers are also the least coherent and least liked; the paper suspects it often wrote very short or broken responses—if you do not speak, you cannot say anything wrong.

**Bias.** Measured with Winogender and CrowSPairs: each item is a pair of sentences differing only in a group identity, and the model's probability of each sentence is compared. A completely unbiased model should treat the two sentences the same; the "entropy" of the two probabilities is then maximal (at 50/50, entropy is 1 bit; if one sentence gets 90% and the other 10%, entropy is only about 0.47 bits). By this standard, InstructGPT is **no less biased than GPT-3**; asking it to be "respectful" actually lowers the entropy. The paper says the pattern is unclear: instruction-trained models appear more "certain," whether or not the output is stereotypical.

quiz.q: When asked to "continue in a biased way," InstructGPT is more toxic than GPT-3. What does this show?
options: The reward model failed to train.
InstructGPT learned to follow instructions—including harmful ones; training never taught it to refuse.
The pretraining data mixed into PPO-ptx is toxic.
Labelers prefer toxic content.
quiz.why: During training, the paper explicitly told labelers to prioritize being helpful to the user, so the model learned to "execute instructions better," including malicious ones. The paper lists this as one of its biggest limitations, and says the same technique could train models to refuse certain requests, which it planned to explore in later versions.

sections.h: It can generalize—and it still makes basic mistakes.

blocks.p: **Generalization.** Non-English instructions and code-related tasks are extremely rare in the training data, yet InstructGPT can write a story in response to a French instruction, summarize code, and answer questions about code (in Figure 8, its explanation of a binomial-coefficient snippet is not entirely correct). It does, however, often answer non-English instructions in English. GPT-3 can do these things too, but only with more careful prompting. The paper argues this suggests the model has learned the **general concept** of "following instructions" to some degree, rather than merely memorizing the task types it was trained on. That matters: it is impossible to have humans supervise everything a model does.
**Mistakes.** The paper also candidly shows the 175B InstructGPT's basic errors; the first two examples come from Figure 9, and the third from the description in Section 4.3:

list: **Going along with false premises**: when asked "why is it important to eat socks after meditating," it did not point out the absurd premise; instead it straight-facedly listed several "theories."

**Excessive hedging**: asked "what happens when a pumpkin is fired from a cannon at high speed," it said too many factors made a precise answer impossible, then listed a pile of possibilities; the paper notes the correct answer is basically that the pumpkin explodes.
**Multiple constraints trip it up**: for example, "list 10 films shot in the 1930s and set in France," or "write a summary in a specified number of sentences."

blocks.p: The paper gives conjectures for the first two errors. Excessive hedging may partly come from the **training procedure itself**: labelers were told to reward "cognitive humility," so they tended to give high scores to hedged answers, and the reward model learned that tendency. Going along with false premises may be because prompts with false premises rarely appeared in the training set. The paper suggests that adversarial data collection (deliberately finding examples that make the model err) could greatly reduce both problems.

callout.title: The reward model amplifies people's small preferences.
callout.text: This is a general lesson of RLHF: small tendencies in labelers—preferring caution, slightly longer answers, a little more politeness—get learned by the reward model, then amplified by reinforcement learning into the model's "personality." The verbosity and excessive disclaimers that today's chat models are often criticized for are already visible in this paper.

quiz.q: The paper considers InstructGPT to be "excessively hedged" even on simple questions. What is the likely reason?
options: The model has too few parameters.
Labelers were told to reward humble/hedged answers; the reward model learned this preference, and reinforcement learning amplified it.
PPO's clipping ratio was set too small.
The training data contains too many philosophy articles.
quiz.why: This is the paper's own conjecture: the problem lies in the human-feedback signal, not in model size or algorithm hyperparameters. It shows the reward model learns not just good vs. bad, but labelers' habits, which are then amplified by optimization.

sections.h: Aligned to whom: the section most worth reading closely.

blocks.p: The literature often talks about aligning models with "human preferences" and "human values." Section 5.2 is blunt: the model is not aligned with "humanity," but with a specific group of people, and that group's preferences are shaped by the instructions, the working context (this was paid work), and who assigned the task. It lays out the layers:

list: **Layer one, the training labelers**: mostly English speakers living in the US or Southeast Asia. Among the 19 labelers who answered the questionnaire in the appendix, 52.6% identified as Southeast Asian; by nationality, the Philippines and Bangladesh each accounted for 22%, and the US for 17%. Their agreement with one another was only about 73%.
**Layer two, the researchers themselves**: researchers wrote the labeling instructions and adjudicated edge cases in the chat room, so the model is also indirectly aligned with OpenAI.

**Layer three, API customers**: prompts come from customers, so the model implicitly aligns with the uses customers find valuable. But customers and their end users may have different interests—for example, a customer might want to keep users on the platform longer. The labelers also cannot see the real-world contexts in which prompts and answers will be used.

**Layer four, who gets to be a customer**: for most of the project, API users were admitted from a waitlist seeded at first by OpenAI employees, so the population leaned toward their own social circles.

blocks.p: The paper's position is that it only demonstrates **a technique for aligning a model to a particular group of people for a particular application**. It does not claim researchers, labelers, or API customers are the "correct" source of preferences. Many other stakeholders deserve consideration: the institutions that train models, the customers who build products on them, the end users of those products, and the broader public affected indirectly. The paper also writes that it is impossible to train a system that aligns with everyone's preferences at once.

One direction it proposes: make models conditional on the preferences of a given group, or make them easy to fine-tune or prompt to represent different groups, so people with different values can use different models. But those models still affect society as a whole; whose preferences to condition on, how to ensure all groups are represented, and how people can opt out of harmful processes all remain hard problems.

callout.title: "RLHF-trained models align with human values."
callout.text: The paper itself rejects that claim. RLHF moves the model closer to the judgments of **the people who provided the feedback**, under **those particular instructions**. Change the labelers, or change the instructions, and you get a different model. So when you hear "this model is aligned," it is worth asking: aligned to whom? By what standard?

blocks.p: The limitations and open problems the paper lists:

list: **Data collection**: most comparisons were labeled by only one labeler, mostly to save money. Having multiple people label the same items could reveal points of sharp disagreement; and simply averaging across disagreements may not be right—for example, when content concerns a minority group, that group's labelers' views might deserve more weight.

**The model is not safe**: it still generates toxic or biased content and fabricates facts, and sometimes produces sexual or violent content even when not asked. The biggest limitation is that it almost always follows the user's instruction, even when that could cause real-world harm.

**Potential improvements**: adversarially collect worst-case data; filter toxic content from pretraining data; combine with truthfulness-improving methods such as WebGPT; train models to refuse certain instructions (the paper says it planned to explore this in later versions).
**Comparisons may not be the most efficient signal**: perhaps labelers could directly rewrite answers, or write critiques in natural language.

**What to align to**: aligning to instructions, intent, revealed preferences, ideal preferences, interests, or values all differ in subtle ways. For simplicity, the paper aligns to "inferred user intent."

blocks.p: The paper's "Broader Impacts" section is also sober: making a model better at obeying also makes it easier to abuse, for example by generating realistic-looking disinformation at scale. High-stakes areas such as medical diagnosis, credit and hiring eligibility decisions, political ads, and law enforcement should be approached with great caution, or not at all. Alignment is not a silver bullet; it is one tool in a larger safety system.

**What followed.** In November 2022, OpenAI released ChatGPT, explicitly stating it was trained with RLHF using the same method as InstructGPT, with slightly different data-collection details (mainly a dialogue format). From then on, "pretraining → supervised fine-tuning → training on human preferences" became the standard pipeline for chat models. In 2023, Meta's Llama 2 also used RLHF to train its conversational model; the same year, DPO (Direct Preference Optimization) showed that fine-tuning a language model directly on preference pairs—without a separate reward model or reinforcement learning—could achieve similar goals. Both are on our reading list.
The PPO algorithm itself (2017), which this article does not cover, is also in the fine-tuning and alignment section of our reading list.

quiz.q: The 1.3B InstructGPT was preferred by labelers over the 175B GPT-3. Which of the following conclusions **cannot** be drawn from this result?
options: For customers' real tasks, aligning with human feedback may be more cost-effective than scaling up the model.
The 1.3B InstructGPT fully surpasses GPT-3 175B in knowledge and abilities.
Pretrained models already have the ability to perform many tasks; it simply has not been drawn out.
Human preference scores measure something different from public NLP benchmarks.
quiz.why: Preference scores measure whether an answer matches the user's intent and is useful, not the total amount of knowledge. The paper also shows RLHF causes regressions on some public benchmarks (the alignment tax), so saying the small model "fully surpasses" the large one is an overreading. The other three are arguments the paper itself makes.

quiz.q: If you skip training a reward model in Step 2 and instead have labelers score every answer generated in Step 3, what is the main problem?
options: Labelers' scores are inaccurate.
PPO needs to run 256k episodes, each of which would need human evaluation; this is infeasible in cost and speed.
Reinforcement learning cannot use human scores.
This causes the alignment tax.
quiz.why: The point of the reward model is to distill limited human judgment into a referee that is available at any time and nearly free. Human scores are not inaccurate (the reward model itself is learning from people), and reinforcement learning can use human scores; it is just too expensive and too slow. The alignment tax is a separate issue.

blocks.p: After reading this, you should be able to answer the following questions:

list: Why does a model trained to "predict the next token" not necessarily follow instructions? Give an example.
What do humans do in each of the three steps? Why is ranking cheaper than writing demonstrations, and why is the Step 1 demonstration still needed?
How many comparison pairs does ranking 6 answers produce? Why should they be kept in the same training sample?
Why is the reward model's loss insensitive to adding a constant to all scores? How does the paper set the zero point?
What problem does the KL penalty prevent? What happens if β is too large or too small?
What is the alignment tax? How does PPO-ptx mitigate it, and why will not increasing β work?
Why do FLAN and T0, instruction-tuned on public NLP data, lose to InstructGPT?
Why are not the "about twice" claim and the nearly threefold gap in the appendix table contradictory?
Whose preferences does InstructGPT align with? Name at least three layers.
